## The question

[Function different from original by differentiating it and integrating it again.](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3606771/function-different-from-original-by-differentiating-it-and-integrating-it-again), asked by [TheQuestioner](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/556133/thequestioner) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2020-04-02; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Let a function be defined $f(x)=sin^4x+cos^4x,$ $x\in R$.<br>Rewriting this,
> $$f(x)=(sin^2x+cos^2x)^2-2sin^2xcos^2x$$$$\implies f(x)=1-\frac{sin^22x}{2}$$$$\implies \frac{1}{2}\leq f(x)\leq1$$
>
> However,upon differentiating the function,we get$$f'(x)=4sin^3x cosx-4cos^3xsinx$$$$\implies f'(x)=4cosxsinx(sin^2x-cos^2x)$$$$\implies f'(x)=-2sin2xcos2x$$$$\implies f'(x)=-sin4x$$Integrating both sides,$$f(x)=\frac{cos4x}{4}$$which lies between$\frac{-1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$and is not equal to the original function.Why is the answer different?
:::

I graphed $x\mapsto \sin^4 x + \cos^4 x$ and $x \mapsto \frac{1}{4}\cos4x$ on the same axes, and here's what I saw.
